stops.title: Lock the dial, then call her pack.
stops.silver: Silver starts paying for each step, then adds a discount: a reward that waits counts for less. Add up everything one run collects, each reward shrunk once for every step it waited, and you have the return.
stops.do: The game is waiting on the dial at the right of the screen. Press F to turn it to a setting and R to lock it in. Then answer with left click for the mini or right click for the mega.
stops.predict: Before you lock it, decide which pack a Tracer who discounts that much walks to: 15 three pads away, or 50 ten pads away.
stops.saw: Each pack showed what it is worth from where she stands: its size, shrunk by the dial once per pad. So 15 x dial^3 against 50 x dial^10. The bot walked to the bigger number, no feelings involved. That dial is the discount factor, gamma: how much one step later is worth compared with now.
stops.agent: A language-model agent turns the same dial: answer now with what it has, or keep calling tools for a better answer later.

stops.title: Try a second setting.
stops.silver: A return is one run's total. With a discount below 1, a reward far down the road barely adds to it, because it gets shrunk again at every step on the way.
stops.do: Press F until the dial shows a setting you have not tried, then R to lock it. Answer with left click for the mini or right click for the mega.
stops.predict: Say whether this setting is more patient or less patient than the last one, and whether that flips her choice.
stops.saw: Both numbers moved, and the mega moved more. It gets shrunk ten times on the way, the mini only three. Her return is everything she collects, each reward shrunk by gamma once per step of delay. Here that is a single pack, so her return is just that pack's shrunk worth.

stops.title: Find where her choice flips.
stops.silver: A state's value is the return you get from it on average. In his example one class is worth far more once the discount lets the big reward ahead count. Patience changes the price.
stops.do: Turn the dial with F to a third setting and lock it with R. Answer with left click for the mini or right click for the mega.
stops.predict: Pick her pack, and guess whether the start is worth more or less to her than at your last setting.
stops.saw: The row did not change. The packs did not change. Only gamma did, and that alone can flip her choice. Below a discount of about 0.84 the mini is worth more; above it, the mega (15 x gamma^3 equals 50 x gamma^10 when gamma^7 is 0.3). So the best policy, the rule for choosing, depends on how patient you are.

stops.title: Lock the last setting.
stops.silver: Turn the discount to 0 and a state is worth only its next reward. Turn it near 1 and the big reward far ahead counts almost in full. Same world, very different price tags.
stops.do: One setting is left. Press R to lock it (F has nothing new to turn to), then answer with left click for the mini or right click for the mega.
stops.predict: You have three answers already; say what the last one is, and why, before you click.
stops.saw: Four settings, one clean split: the mini won at 0.5 and 0.8, the mega at 0.9 and 1. The coach line then gave Silver's reasons to discount: the far future is less certain, sums over endless steps stay finite, and sooner is usually worth more. A discount of 1 is safe here because every walk ends at a pack.

stops.title: Say what her state must hold.
stops.silver: A policy, the rule for choosing, looks only at the current state. Silver says that is enough, as long as the state carries everything about the past that matters.
stops.do: A question floats in front of you. Left click: yes, both. Right click: here yes, match no. Melee: no, not here.
stops.predict: Decide whether knowing only her pad tells you all you need about what comes next, on this island and in a real match.
stops.saw: On this row nothing changes but where she stands, so her pad is a Markov state: know it, and the past adds nothing. A real match is less polite. A taken pack comes back on a timer, so two Tracers on the same pad can face different futures. The fix from lecture 1, which Silver repeats with his counter, is to put the timer into the state.
stops.agent: An agent that sees only the last message is Tracer without the timer. It needs the history in its state, or a summary of it.

stops.title: Fill the pads, then walk them.
stops.silver: Pick a policy and keep it. Then a state's value is the next step's reward plus the discounted value of wherever that step leads, averaged over your choices and the world's dice.
stops.do: Press F to fill the pads. Each step now costs 1 and the discount is 0.9. Three pads get numbers, then a question asks for the pad marked ?: left click, right click or melee. Then walk the row to the mega with WASD.
stops.predict: Work out the ? pad from the pad ahead of it before you click.
stops.saw: Each number is what that pad is worth if she always walks to the mega. Start from 50 at the mega and walk backwards: minus 1 for the step, plus 0.9 times the pad ahead. The line on the right checked it on every pad you stood on, down to 10.92 at the start. You just did the Bellman expectation equation with your feet.
stops.agent: Your guess at whether an agent's task will pass from here follows the same rule: the cost of one more tool call, plus the discounted guess after it.

stops.title: Switch her rule to the mini.
stops.silver: Every state has a ceiling: the most any policy at all could get from there, which Silver calls its optimal value. Once you know it, playing well is easy: take the action that reaches it.
stops.do: You are back on the start pad. The question asks whether the start pad is worth more or less than 10.92 if she always walks to the mini instead: left click for more, right click for less.
stops.predict: Decide which way the number moves when only her way of walking changes.
stops.saw: Same pad, new rule, new number: 8.23 walking to the mini, against 10.92 walking to the mega. Then the pads redrew for the mini walk, and one pad behind the start the mini walk won, 10.25 against 8.83. So the best policy is not one walk. It takes, pad by pad, whichever walk is worth more from there.

stops.title: Read the debrief.
stops.silver: The best values obey the same one-step look ahead with one change: take the best of your own moves instead of averaging them. That max is why they need repeated sweeps instead of one matrix inverse.
stops.do: Press F for the debrief. Three lines appear on the left, and your prediction score sits under the title.
stops.predict: Before you press, count how many of the seven predictions you think you got right.
stops.saw: The lines name what you did: the discount, the return as a discounted sum, value under a policy, and the Bellman equation. One thing the game quietly skipped is the dice. Every step lands where it aims, so the average over next states has one term. In Silver's examples a chance node puts a probability-weighted average there.
stops.agent: Turn an agent's discount down and it answers from what it already has. Turn it up and it will happily spend more tool calls chasing a better answer.
